Richard the Lionheart and Philip of France ate off the same plate every day, and at night their beds did not separate them.

A treaty you could nap in.

Historians have argued about it since 1948. Richard never explained himself. He didn't have to.

Would you sign a treaty like that?

She was on trial for her life in Ancient Athens — and her defense left the entire courtroom speechless.

Phryne was the most famous courtesan in Greece. The priests accused her of blasphemy, and the penalty was death. When her lawyer Hypereides realized his words weren't landing, he did the unthinkable — he tore her robe open and argued that only the gods could carve a body that perfect.

The judges froze. They set her free.

Two thousand years later, historians still argue about whether it really happened.

Would you have dared it?

One gesture. That's all it took to overturn a death sentence in Ancient Athens.

Phryne was the most famous courtesan in Greece — beautiful enough that sculptors used her as the model for Aphrodite herself. Then the priests accused her of blasphemy, a crime that carried the death penalty.

Her lawyer begged the jury. Their faces didn't move. So he tore her robe open and told the court that only the gods could carve a body that perfect — and killing her would be an insult to them.

The judges froze. She walked free.

Historians still can't agree whether it actually happened.

Would you have dared it?

The secret police watched his apartment and counted the women going inside. Dozens. Every single day. Duchesses and prostitutes in the same queue.

Grigori Rasputin, a Siberian peasant, taught noblewomen that salvation came through sin — the more you sinned, the holier you got. Some kept his dirty underwear as holy relics.

Then he reached the palace. The heir to Russia was a haemophiliac, and this filthy peasant mystic was the only man who could stop the bleeding. The Tsarina worshipped him.

So they decided to kill him. Poisoned cakes. Poisoned wine. He kept eating. They shot him — he got back up. They shot him again and dumped him in the river.

Except none of that happened. The autopsy found no poison, no water in his lungs, and one shot to the forehead. His killer made it up to sell a book.

Three things everyone repeats about the history of this device. All three are false.

Cleopatra and the gourd full of bees? No ancient source says it. The story was invented in 1992.

Archaeologists really did rebuild a 29,000-year-old stone object from 14 fragments. Eight inches long. It was also used as a hammer.

And the Victorian doctor everyone credits with curing hysteria? He refused to treat women with it, and said so in writing. That story traces back to a single book published in 1999. In 2018 historians checked every source it cited. Not one of them said it.

Both of the myths you believe were invented in your lifetime.

#history #historyfacts #victorian #mythbusting #didyouknow

The most repeated fact on this subject has no ancient source at all. It was made up in 1992.

What is real: archaeologists reconstructed a 29,000-year-old stone object from 14 separate fragments. Eight inches long. It had also been used as a hammer.

In 1869 a doctor built a padded table powered by a steam engine so large it lived in the next room and came through the wall. He called it the Manipulator.

And the man everyone credits with curing hysteria in 1880? He refused to use it on women and wrote that down. The whole story comes from one book published in 1999. Historians checked its sources in 2018. Not one supported it.

caption:
In 1944, Germany's highest military honour was personally awarded to a spy operating in Britain. The spy had been working for the British the entire time.

Juan Pujol Garcia was a chicken farmer from Barcelona who hated fascism. He offered to spy for Britain. Britain turned him down three times, so he went and offered himself to the other side instead.

They sent him to London. He never went. He wrote his reports from Lisbon using a tourist guide, a railway timetable and old newsreels, and they believed every word.

When Britain finally realised what he was doing, they hired him too. Together they invented a network of twenty-seven agents. Every one was fictional. Their salaries were paid by the enemy.

In 1944 he swore the invasion would land at Calais. It landed at Normandy.

He is the only person in history to be decorated by both sides.

A bored German engineer drew a chastity belt as a joke in 1405, and it fooled the world for six hundred years.

Konrad Kyeser was writing Bellifortis, a manual of war machines. Between a catapult and a device for turning invisible, he sketched an iron belt for locking up a woman - and wrote underneath that a joke binds the whole series together.

Six centuries later his joke was sitting in museums. Not the drawing. The object.

In the 1800s forgers hammered them out and sold them to collectors as medieval antiques, and the museums bought them. No knight ever owned one. Not one verified example has ever been excavated from the medieval period.

The British Museum now says most were made in the 18th and 19th centuries "as curiosities for the prurient, or as jokes for the tasteless" - and quietly recatalogued its own famous example as Victorian.

Kyeser would have loved that.

Source: Albrecht Classen, The Medieval Chastity Belt: A Myth-Making Process (Palgrave, 2007)

A Viking woman was divorced for wearing trousers. So she put them back on, rode to his house, and stabbed him in his bed.

Iceland, around the year 1000. Aud was married to Thord - until Thord wanted Gudrun, and Gudrun told him exactly how to get out of it.

Icelandic law let you divorce a spouse for dressing as the opposite sex. So Thord stood up at the Althing and announced that Aud wore men's breeches with a codpiece. It worked.

The law cut both ways: a man could be divorced for wearing a shirt cut low enough to show his chest.

Then one night Aud pulled the breeches back on, rode to his farm, walked into his bedroom and put a sword through his arm and chest.

The saga says he lived. He kept the wife. She kept the trousers. And his sword arm never worked properly again.

Told in the Laxdaela saga, chapters 32-35 - a 13th-century saga about 10th-century events. The cross-dressing divorce law itself is attested in Gragas, the Icelandic lawbook.

In 1726 a woman convinced the King's own surgeon that she was giving birth to rabbits.

Mary Toft was a poor cloth worker from Godalming. After a miscarriage she began producing pieces of animal flesh, and the local surgeon John Howard delivered them himself. Nine rabbits, he said. Then more.

Word reached London. George I sent his personal surgeon, Nathaniel St Andre, who watched a delivery, declared it genuine, and rushed a pamphlet into print defending it.

Then Sir Richard Manningham arrived. He watched, he doubted, and he told Mary he intended to operate on her to find out.

She confessed that night. She had been inserting dead rabbits by hand.

Mary was jailed as a "Notorious and Vile Cheat". Nathaniel St Andre, surgeon to the King, never practised again.

The emperor's official historian secretly wrote a book calling him a demon. It surfaced a thousand years later.

Procopius of Caesarea was court historian to Justinian. His public works - the Wars, the Buildings - praised the emperor's campaigns and his architecture.

In private he was writing something else. The Secret History is around a hundred pages of pure rage. One chapter is headed "Proving That Justinian and Theodora Were Actually Fiends in Human Form".

He never published it. If he had, Justinian would have had him executed.

It sat unread for centuries until it turned up in the Vatican Library, and was finally printed in 1623.

Which is worth remembering: almost everything scandalous you have ever heard about Empress Theodora traces back to a book her own court historian was too frightened to publish in his lifetime. It is hostile polemic, not reportage - and historians have argued about how much of it to believe ever since.

#history #historyfacts #byzantine #rome #ancienthistory

A surgeon practised on 75 poor men before he was allowed to operate on the King of France. Not all of them survived.

In 1686 Louis XIV had an anal fistula - an infected tunnel near his backside. Nothing the royal physicians tried worked, and the pain was making it hard for him to sit, walk or ride.

So Charles-Francois Felix, the king's chief surgeon, was ordered to cut it out. There was one problem: he had never performed the operation.

Felix spent months touring the hospitals and prisons of Paris, finding poor men with the same condition and operating on them to practise. Contemporary accounts say not all of them survived.

On 21 November 1686 he operated on the king. Three hours, no anaesthetic. It worked.

And because a surgeon had succeeded where the physicians failed, surgery in France stopped being a barber's trade and started becoming a profession.

They say the Empress of Rome took on 25 men in one night. That story is a poem, not history — written decades after she died by a satirist who hated women.

The real thing was worse. In 48 AD, while Claudius was 16 miles away at Ostia, Messalina held a full public wedding to Gaius Silius. Vows, witnesses, sacrifices, guests. She was still married to the Emperor of Rome. Both she and Silius were dead within a day.

Source: Tacitus, Annals XI.26-38.

The night before her wedding, a medieval bride was told to put leeches inside herself. Not by a criminal — by a medical textbook.

The Trotula was written in Salerno in the 12th century, at the finest medical school in Europe. Between remedies for childbirth and cracked lips, it explains how to fake virginity.

One recipe is a wash of oak apples, alum and comfrey boiled in rainwater — an astringent. It tightens.

But the book says there is something better: "let her place leeches in the vagina (but take care that they do not go in too far) so that blood comes out and is converted into a little clot."

It would break on the wedding night, and everyone would see what they expected to see.

Part of it was written by a woman — Trota of Salerno.

Source: The Trotula, ed. and trans. Monica H. Green (2001).

#history #medieval #middleages #historyfacts #womenshistory

Some historians believe medieval women chose the back door rather than lose their virginity.

Under the Church's purity laws a woman's worth was settled before she ever spoke — handed to a stranger for land or money, and expected to arrive untouched.

We know the Church was worried about something. Bishops wrote handbooks listing every act a priest might hear in confession, each with a penance counted in years of bread and water.

Whether women truly did this, or whether celibate monks only imagined it, historians still argue.

The handbooks survive. The confessions don't.

Everyone's talking about Bonnie Blue. Rome had one two thousand years ago, and she was the Empress.

They say Messalina took on 25 men in a single night and walked away unsatisfied. It isn't true — it's a poem, written decades after she died by a satirist who hated women.

What she actually did was worse. In 48 AD, while Claudius was 16 miles away at Ostia, Messalina held a full public wedding to Gaius Silius. Vows, witnesses, sacrifices, guests. She was still married to the Emperor of Rome. Both were dead by nightfall.

Rome didn't kill her for the rumour. It killed her for the wedding.

Source: Tacitus, Annals XI.26-38.

The Etruscans shared their wives at dinner — and the Greeks never got over it.

If a wife wanted another man at the table, her husband was expected to pour the wine. He just had to accept it.

The Greeks wrote it down in horror: nobody in Etruria knew whose child was whose, and nobody seemed to mind. An Etruscan woman owned property in her own right, kept her own name to the grave, and passed it to her children as though no man had ever been involved.

Rome took their roads, their arches and their gods. Then it took this as well.

Would you have survived an Etruscan dinner party? 👇

caption:
He burned a city to kill his wife — then she opened her robe and he dropped the sword.

For ten years Menelaus told every man at Troy that he would kill his wife with his own hands. The horse put him inside the walls. He went straight through the burning palace to find her.

She did not run, and she did not beg. She let the robe fall open — and the sword went out of his hand and onto the floor.

He took her home to Sparta and put her back on the throne. Homer has her pouring wine for guests as if none of it had ever happened.

Would you have dropped the sword? 👇

note: Rasputin - ARCHIVAL - public-domain photos + Signal Corps 1917 footage
caption:
Russian noblewomen queued outside Rasputin's flat every morning - and it was their husbands who sent them.

Not for the reason the rumours say. They came for favours: promotions, postings, sons pulled out of the war. Rasputin had the Empress's ear, and everyone in Petersburg knew it.

He had earned it doing the one thing Europe's best doctors could not - stopping the heir's bleeding. Alexei was a haemophiliac. Nobody has ever fully explained what Rasputin did at that bedside.

His enemies printed cartoons of him with the Empress in his lap. The story travelled faster than the truth, and it helped bring down a dynasty.

He had a wife back in Siberia. Asked about the other women, she said: he has enough for all.

Every image is a real public-domain photograph. No AI.
